p13: 13.  On 19 August 2008 T. applied to the Family Court of Australia, seeking recognition of his parental rights in respect of the child. In support of his claims, in a written statement made under oath, he stated that he had been in a relationship with the applicant since 2004 and that she had always told him that he was the child’s father; that the applicant’s rental of the flat had been fictitious and the result of an agreement between them; and that he had made false statements to the social-welfare services in order to enable the applicant to receive single-parent benefit. T. asserted that the applicant had left Australian territory with the child without his consent, in breach of Article 3 of the Hague Convention, and had gone to an unknown place of residence in Latvia. In support of his application he produced e-mails exchanged with members of his family.
p14: 14.  The applicant, although apparently invited by various means to attend the hearing or to follow it by telephone, did not appear.
p15: 15.  In a judgment of 6 November 2008 the Australian Family Court established T.’s paternity in respect of the child and held that the applicant and T. had had joint parental responsibility for their daughter since her birth. It added that the examination of the case would continue once the child had been returned to Australia, and stated as follows:
p16: 16.  The applicant did not appeal against that judgment.
p17: 17.  On 22 September 2008 the Ministry of Children and Family Affairs, the Latvian Central Authority responsible for implementing the Hague Convention, received from its Australian counterpart a request by T. for the child’s return to Australia under that international convention. The request for return was accompanied by a written statement made under oath explaining the applicable Australian law and certifying, without prejudging the issue of paternity, that on the date on which the child had been removed from Australia T. had been exercising joint parental responsibility for her within the meaning of Article 5 of the Hague Convention.
p18: 18.  On 19 November 2008 the Zemgale District Court of the City of Rīga (“the District Court”) examined the request in the presence of both T. and the applicant.
p19: 19.  At the hearing the applicant opposed T.’s request. She explained that he had no grounds for being recognised as the father, given that at the time of the birth she had still been married to another man and that T. had never expressed any wish to have his paternity established before her departure from Australia. She submitted that T. had become hostile and sometimes aggressive towards her, and she asked for persons who had visited her in Australia to be summoned as witnesses. The applicant further claimed that T. was using this remedy solely in order to gain an advantage in criminal proceedings which, she alleged, had been brought against him in Australia.
p20: 20.  The representative of the “Bāriņtiesa”, a guardianship and curatorship authority set up by Rīga City Council, asked for T.’s request to be dismissed, arguing, firstly, that the applicant had been a single mother on the date on which the child was removed from Australia and, secondly, that the child had established ties with Latvia.
